name: The Tri-State Tornado
blurb: The longest tornado track ever recorded and the deadliest single tornado in United States history. It pre-dates the national database by twenty-five years, so this track is a reconstruction, not a survey.
source: Reconstructed from the documented sequence of towns struck and the recorded times

sources: Johns et al. (2013), E-Journal of Severe Storms Meteorology 8(2) — 2,433 timed damage records
torn.story: The deadliest tornado in United States history. It touched down around 12:40 PM in Shannon County, Missouri — the 2013 reanalysis moved the start well west of where the old accounts put it — and ran east-northeast for three and a half hours at an average of 60 mph, across the Mississippi into southern Illinois and over the Wabash into Indiana. It destroyed Annapolis and Biehle in Missouri, then Gorham, Murphysboro (234 dead, the most ever in one city), De Soto (33 children at the school), West Frankfort and Parrish in Illinois, and Griffin and Princeton in Indiana. Witnesses rarely saw a funnel: it was a churning black mass of cloud and debris a mile wide, low to the ground, moving too fast to outrun. 695 died.

torn.story: A later tornado from the same storm system, an hour and a quarter after the Tri-State tornado lifted: homes twisted to splinters and farms wrecked across Washington County and into Jackson County along the Muscatatuck bottoms. Not rated.

story: Just after one in the afternoon on 18 March 1925, a tornado touched down in the hills of south-eastern Missouri. For the next three and a half hours it held an almost straight line east-north-east across the corner of Missouri, all of southern Illinois and into Indiana, moving at around sixty miles an hour — faster than anyone in its way could have run from it, on a day when there was no tornado forecasting, no radar and no warning of any kind.
It rarely looked like a tornado. Witnesses described a boiling, rolling mass of cloud on the ground, wrapped in rain and debris, and many did not know what it was until it had passed over them.

Southern Illinois took the worst of it. Gorham was all but erased. In Murphysboro 234 people died, still the most ever killed by a tornado in a single American city, and De Soto lost 69, many of them children at its school. It crossed the Wabash into Indiana, destroyed Griffin, and lifted near Petersburg late in the afternoon.

Whether it was one tornado the whole way was argued about for most of a century. The 2013 reanalysis by Johns and colleagues, working from newspaper accounts, photographs and the original damage reports, concluded it was very probably a single tornado for at least 174 miles and possibly for as much as 235. The track here follows that reconstruction.
